property_summary: Only the Owner can cause c.withdraw() to transfer out the contract balance (i.e., after calling withdraw the contract balance is zero iff msg.sender was Owner).
Only calls to withdraw originated from the contract's Owner do not revert (i.e., withdraw reverts for non-owners).
If the caller is not c.Owner(), then the call to c.withdraw() must have reverted.
If msg.sender is not c.Owner(), then the call to c.withdraw() must have reverted.
If the caller is not c.Owner(), then the call to c.withdraw() must have reverted.

For all callers and inputs, only the Owner can cause the contract balance to be sent out by calling withdraw (i.e., calling withdraw does not change the contract balance when msg.sender != Owner); the mutant removing the require allows non-owners to drain the contract and thus violates this property for some inputs.

For every caller and inputs, if the contract balance is nonzero then a call to Command(...) by a non-Owner must not enable that caller to reduce address(c).balance (only the Owner withdrawing should change balance); the mutant removing the withdraw require allows a non-Owner to cause the contract balance to be drained after invoking Command routed through a re-entrant helper, violating this rule for some inputs.

For any caller and any calldata/ETH sent to Command, if the caller is not Owner then after calling Command the contract balance remains unchanged in the reference (only Owner can cause the contract to lose balance by calling withdraw), but the mutant (which makes withdraw callable by anyone) allows some non-Owner interactions to result in a decreased contract balance.

For every non-owner caller and for any calldata/ETH they send to Command routed through a reverting callee, executing Command cannot make withdraw succeed for that non-owner (i.e., only the Owner can successfully call withdraw); the mutant (which removes the require in withdraw) allows a non-owner to drain the contract after provoking a reentrant/failing interaction, violating this rule for some fuzzed inputs.

For all callers and calldata, if a non-Owner calls Command targeting a contract whose fallback consumes the forwarded ETH but does NOT itself call back into C, then after Command returns the contract balance is unchanged in the reference (only Owner can withdraw later), whereas the mutant (which makes withdraw callable by anyone) can allow a subsequent withdraw by that same non-Owner to transfer away the balance — so the invariant: non-Owner cannot later successfully withdraw C's balance after calling Command with any calldata/ETH to a non-reentrant callee.
After funding C and then calling withdraw from this contract, the contract balance becomes zero (Owner can be paid out), which holds for P but is violated when withdraw requires non-Owner callers.
When the caller is the contract's Owner, calling withdraw must revert (only Owner may withdraw in original).
If msg.sender == c.Owner(), then calling c.withdraw() must revert.
If msg.sender equals c.Owner(), then calling c.withdraw() must revert (i.e. the assertion checks that when msg.sender == owner, reverted is true).
If msg.sender equals c.Owner(), then calling c.withdraw() must revert.

For all callers and balances, the original contract ensures that the contract balance can be withdrawn to Owner when Owner calls withdraw (i.e., Owner can successfully empty the contract); the mutant inverts the require so Owner calls will be rejected and thus fails to withdraw for some inputs.

For any caller and any balance, the original contract allows the Owner to successfully call withdraw and empty the contract (withdraw call by Owner does not revert and leaves contract balance at 0); the mutant inverts the require so Owner's withdraw reverts for some inputs, breaking this property.

For any caller address and any nonzero ether amount sent into C via Command to increase its balance, the contract’s Owner can always successfully call withdraw and after the call the contract balance is zero; the mutant inverts the require so the Owner cannot withdraw and this property can be violated.

For any caller address and any non-negative ether amount deposited into C, when the contract Owner calls withdraw the call succeeds and leaves the contract balance zero; the mutant inverts the require so Owner cannot call withdraw and thus can fail to empty the balance for some inputs.

For any nonzero ether amount and the contract Owner as caller, calling withdraw succeeds and leaves the contract balance at zero; the mutant inverts the require so Owner's withdraw will revert and can leave balance nonzero for some inputs.

For any caller who is the stored Owner, calling withdraw always sends the entire contract balance to the stored Owner (so address(c).balance becomes 0 and Owner's balance increases); the mutant sending to msg.sender can send funds to a different address and thus can leave address(c).balance != 0 for some fuzzed caller/payment scenario.

For any caller X that is the stored Owner and for any contract balance B≥0, after Owner calls withdraw the contract balance becomes 0 (all funds are sent to the Owner); the mutant that sends to msg.sender can break this by making the caller differ from Owner so funds do not leave the contract when withdraw is invoked under that caller identity.

For any caller who is the stored Owner and any nonnegative contract balance, after Owner calls withdraw the contract's balance becomes zero (all funds are forwarded to Owner); the mutant that forwards to msg.sender breaks this by still leaving nonzero balance when Owner is not the recipient of the transfer (i.e., when the transfer target differs).

For every caller who is the stored Owner, calling withdraw transfers the contract's entire balance out of the contract (address(c).balance == 0) — the mutant that uses msg.sender as transfer target can break this when Owner != msg.sender in the transfer (i.e., if transfer target differs), so some admissible input (a fuzzed caller address not equal to stored Owner) will make address(c).balance != 0 after withdraw on the mutant.

For any caller who is the stored Owner and for any contract balance, when Owner calls withdraw the contract balance becomes zero (all funds are sent out); the mutant that sends to msg.sender instead of Owner can break this by leaving funds in the contract when the caller is the Owner but msg.sender differs from Owner (i.e., if the transfer target is not the stored Owner).

For any caller who is the Owner and when the contract has a positive balance, calling withdraw transfers the entire contract balance to Owner (so address(c).balance becomes 0); the mutant that changes transfer(amount) to transfer(0) violates this because the contract balance remains nonzero after withdraw for some inputs.

For any caller equal to Owner who sends at least some wei to the contract beforehand, calling withdraw empties the contract (address(c).balance == 0); the mutant that changes transfer(...) to transfer(0) can leave a nonzero balance, violating this rule.

For any caller Owner and any nonzero contract balance, calling withdraw transfers all contract balance to Owner (making address(c).balance == 0); the mutant that replaces transfer(address(this).balance) with transfer(0) can leave a nonzero contract balance after withdraw, thus violating this property for some inputs.

If the owner calls withdraw when the contract has a positive balance, then after the call the contract balance becomes zero; the mutant that changes transfer(...) to transfer(0) can leave a positive contract balance, violating this rule for some inputs.

If Owner calls withdraw when the contract has a positive balance and Owner is a contract that reverts on receiving Ether, the reference C's withdraw will revert (so call fails) while the mutant that transfers 0 will succeed; thus for all admissible inputs the reference either transfers full balance (succeeds) or reverts when the recipient reverts, but the mutant can succeed while reference reverts — detect by comparing call success.

For any caller and any contract balance, calling withdraw() as the Owner always results in the contract's entire balance being forwarded out (address(c).balance == 0) in the correct contract; the mutant that replaces transfer with an unchecked low-level call can leave funds in the contract when the destination call fails.
Calling Command with a target address that reverts must NOT cause the transaction to revert and should leave caller's execution continuing (i.e., Command returns normally / does not revert).
Calling c.Command with given inputs should not cause the test to revert and execution must reach the final assert that address(c).balance <= address(this).balance + value.
After calling c.Command, the test asserts that address(c).balance <= address(this).balance + value remains true.
Calling c.Command with the given inputs must not revert and execution must reach the final assert that address(c).balance <= address(this).balance + value.
Calling c.Command with the given inputs does not revert and execution reaches the final assert that address(c).balance <= address(this).balance + value.

For any caller and calldata, when the contract's Command is invoked by the Owner, the reference C never reverts because it ignores a callee's failure (call returns false but Command returns normally); the mutant that requires success will revert for inputs where the callee deliberately fails, breaking this property.
